chunks: Musa ibn al-Qasim from Muhammad ibn Sahl from his father from Isḥāq ibn ʿAbd Allāh said:

I asked Abū al-Ḥasan (peace be upon him) about the resident of Mecca who performs Hajj exclusively (Qirān) or performs Tamattuʾ for another time, so he said: 'I prefer that he performs Tamattuʾ, and his iḥrām should be from a journey of one night or two nights. If he limits himself to his ʿUmrah in Rajab, he is not considered a Mutamattiʾ, and if he is not a Mutamattiʾ, the sacrifice (ḥady) is not obligatory upon him.'

It is also permissible that the meaning is to emphasize the superiority (of the act), because whoever resides in Mecca and has performed ʿUmrah in Rajab, it is superior for him to offer a sacrifice, even if he does not do so, nothing is upon him. If the Mutamattiʾ is a slave and has performed Hajj with his master's permission, then his master has the choice: if he wishes, he slaughters on his behalf, and if he wishes, he orders him to fast. Narrated.

key_terms.مَسِيرَةِ لَيْلَةٍ: A journey of one night (distance required to exit miqāt)
key_terms.يَتَمَتَّعُ: Performs Tamattuʾ (a type of Hajj where one performs Umrah and Hajj with separate iḥrām)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on the sacrifice (hady) for a resident of Mecca performing Hajj, and does performing Umrah in Rajab count as Tamattu?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi records Imam al-Rida’s (AS) preference for the Tamattuʾ form of Hajj for Mecca residents, provided they perform a distinct Umrah from a miqāt rather than just an Umrah in Rajab, thereby clarifying the conditions for the obligatory sacrifice (hady). The narration further elucidates the juristic flexibility for a slave’s master, who may choose between offering a sacrifice or commanding fasting, reflecting the practical application of ritual obligations in domestic and social contexts.
